what_it_does: In chip manufacturing, "yield" is the fraction of chips coming off the production line that actually work correctly; maximizing yield means tweaking dozens of design parameters to make the circuit robust against the tiny, unavoidable random variations that occur during fabrication. Finding good parameter settings requires running large numbers of computer simulations of the manufacturing process — each simulation is expensive. Current optimization methods waste budget by spending just as much compute on clearly bad designs as on promising ones. This paper proposes a smarter framework that uses a statistical model (a Continuous AutoRegression model) to learn how much a quick, approximate simulation agrees with a slow, high-fidelity one. Armed with that learned relationship, it applies more compute only to the most promising design candidates and uses cheaper approximations elsewhere, converging to a good solution in fewer than 1,000 total simulations rather than the tens of thousands that exhaustive methods would need.
